Memory Jogger.new: A Sri Lankan asylum seeker caught 25 yards inside the border could not use habeas to challenge his negative credible-fear finding: the Court held 7--2 that the Suspension Clause protects release from unlawful custody, not further review of a claim to stay, and that an alien at the threshold of entry has only the procedural rights Congress grants (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/591/19-161/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court \textbf{reversed and remanded with instructions to dismiss} by a \textbf{7--2} vote. The case was argued on March 2, 2020, and decided on June 25, 2020 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/591/19-161/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/19-161}{Cornell LII}):

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (No Habeas Review): A Border-Adjacent Credible-Fear Denial.}

Examples: Future Applications.from: Under \textit{Thuraissigiam}, the district court must dismiss

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (No Habeas Review): An Asylum Seeker at a Port of Entry.} A noncitizen without valid documents presents herself at a land port of entry and asks for asylum. She is placed in expedited removal, and an asylum officer and an immigration judge find no credible fear. In a habeas petition she argues that her interview was conducted through an interpreter who spoke a different dialect, and she asks for a new interview. Like Thuraissigiam, she seeks another chance at admission rather than simple release, so the Suspension Clause does not require review. And because she has never entered the United States, she has only the procedural rights Congress has provided by statute; the Court stressed that a clandestine entrant should not receive more process than such a port-of-entry applicant (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/591/19-161/}{Justia}).
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Habeas Available): Core Release From Interior Detention.}

Examples: Future Applications.from: Suppose instead DHS arrests a noncitizen

Examples: Future Applications.src: Unlike \textit{Thuraissigiam}, this statute violates both the Suspension Clause and the Due Process Clause. The petitioner seeks \textit{simple release from unlawful executive detention}---the indisputable 1789 core of the Great Writ recognized in \textit{Thuraissigiam}, \textit{St. Cyr}, and \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/553/723/}{\textit{Boumediene}}
an established U.S. resident (or citizen) inside the country holds full Fifth Amendment due process protections against arbitrary detention and summary removal

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Habeas Available): A Claim of Citizenship.} A man apprehended near the border is placed in expedited removal and ordered removed after a negative credible-fear finding. In a habeas petition he asserts that he is a United States citizen, born in Texas, and offers a birth certificate. Section 1252(e)(2) itself permits habeas review of whether the petitioner is an alien and whether he is a lawful permanent resident, refugee, or asylee, so the district court has jurisdiction to decide his citizenship claim. Nothing in \textit{Thuraissigiam} forecloses that inquiry: a citizen wrongly subjected to expedited removal is not an alien seeking initial admission, and his challenge is to the Executive's power to hold and remove him at all.

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Unresolved): Expedited Removal Deep in the Interior.} DHS arrests a noncitizen in Chicago who entered without inspection and has lived there for eighteen months, places him in expedited removal under the statute's two-year presence limit, and denies his credible-fear claim. He files a habeas petition arguing that the asylum officer applied the wrong legal standard and that he is entitled to full due process. The Suspension Clause holding cuts against him because he seeks further review rather than release. But the due process holding rested on Thuraissigiam's status at the threshold of initial entry, and the Court did not say when presence inside the country matures into an entry carrying fuller constitutional protection (see \textit{Zadvydas v.\ Davis}, 533 U.S.\ 678 (2001)). Whether eighteen months of residence is enough remains open.
